newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Nobel peace awards put East Timor in spotlight.
newsitem.headline: Nobel peace awards put East Timor in spotlight.

text.p: The joint award of the Nobel Peace Prize to an East Timor bishop and an independence activist on Friday has placed the troubled territory annexed by Indonesia 20 years ago firmly back under the international spotlight.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee gave the prize to Roman Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo and self-exiled independence movement spokesman Jose Ramos-Horta "for their work towards a just and peaceful solution to the conflict in East Timor".

Diplomatic and political analysts said it would be hard for the Indonesian government to swallow, and might even delay peace efforts in the former Portuguese territory which Indonesia has ruled since its December 1975 invasion.
"It's a difficult decision for Indonesia," a diplomatic source said.
"In a sense it represents the acknowledgement of the international community that Indonesia's claims to successful integration (of East Timor) haven't been accepted," he said.
"It probably now means a problem of damage limitation for Indonesia," another source said.
The United Nations has refused to accept Indonesia's claim to East Timor and still regards former colonial ruler Portugal as the administering power.
Indonesia's State Secretary Murdiono, who is close to President Suharto, told reporters in what he said was a private capacity that he was surprised by the award.
"I don't understand what were the criteria by which they chose them," he said.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Ghaffar Fadyl said: "It is the right of the committee with its own criteria to award the Nobel Peace Prize. However, we regret that a political opportunist has received the prize" -- a reference to Ramos-Horta.
Some diplomatic sources were puzzled at the inclusion of Ramos-Horta, who lives in Sydney, Australia.
"It is hard to see how he managed to get the prize...he hasn't actually been involved in the peace process," one said.

Analysts said the Nobel award could also strengthen Lisbon's campaign against Indonesia to try to force a U.N.-sponsored self-determination vote in the territory. Jakarta has consistently rejected such a poll, saying the East Timorese themselves had sought integration.
There was concern too that hardliners in Indonesia could see the award as proof of their fears of an international conspiracy against their country
Diplomatic analysts said the future depended to an extent on how the two prize winners reacted and what they said.
Belo, who was saying a Mass in a school in the capital Dili when the award was announced, quickly spoke of peace and reconciliation.
"I see it as a victory for East Timorese...and all Indonesian," he told Reuters. "Peace can be achieved through non-violent means."

Ramos-Horta, who was secretary for foreign affairs and information in the leftist Fretilin movement and fled three days before the 1975 invasion, said his share of the prize should have gone to Xanana Gusmao, the resistance leader now serving a 20-year sentence in an Indonesian prison.
Bishop Belo also said in reacting to the news that he hoped there would be no rejoicing in East Timor. He did not elaborate.
But diplomatic sources feared the award could inflame anti-Christian feeling in some areas of the sprawling archipelago of nearly 200 million people, over 85 percent of them Moslem.
Police said five people died when a rampaging mob in eastern Java burned nine churches, several schools and a convent on Thursday.

A local reporter said the violence apparently started after several thousand people demanded that a man being tried in court for alleged blasphemy against Islam be sentenced immediately or handed over to the crowd.
